params.question: Why is a pregnant woman with pre-existing heart disease at the greatest risk of cardiac decompensation between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation?

answers.text: Because the foetus begins producing its own blood supply, increasing placental vascular resistance

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Foetal haematopoiesis begins much earlier and does not directly increase maternal cardiac workload. The risk at 28–32 weeks is driven by the peak in maternal blood volume and cardiac output.

answers.text: Because maternal haemodynamic changes — blood volume and cardiac output — peak at this gestational age, imposing the maximum cardiac workload

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Blood volume rises by 40–50% and cardiac output by 30–50%, peaking at 28–32 weeks. A heart with a fixed obstruction such as mitral stenosis cannot accommodate this additional load, leading to decompensation.

answers.text: Because progesterone levels decline after 28 weeks, removing their vasodilatory protective effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Progesterone remains elevated throughout pregnancy and continues to promote vasodilation. The risk at 28–32 weeks arises from peak circulatory demands, not from hormonal withdrawal.

answers.text: Because the gravid uterus directly compresses the heart at this stage of pregnancy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava in the supine position (aortocaval compression), but it does not compress the heart itself. The increased risk is due to peak haemodynamic demands on the myocardium.

overallFeedback.feedback: The haemodynamic adaptations of pregnancy — increased blood volume, cardiac output, and heart rate — reach their maximum at 28–32 weeks. A diseased heart with limited reserve cannot accommodate this peak workload, which is why close surveillance is essential during this period.
Well done. The cardiovascular system reaches peak strain at 28–32 weeks, making this the critical window for monitoring women with cardiac disease.

params.question: Why is a structured antenatal screening protocol considered essential for the detection of gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM)?

answers.text: Because GDM presents with dramatic symptoms that require laboratory confirmation before treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: GDM is characteristically asymptomatic. Polyuria and polydipsia may occasionally occur but are non-specific and unreliable. The absence of symptoms is precisely why screening is essential.

answers.text: Because the oral glucose tolerance test can only be performed during a narrow two-week gestational window

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While screening is timed to specific gestational ages (commonly 24–28 weeks), the rationale for a structured protocol is the asymptomatic nature of GDM, not a narrow laboratory window.

answers.text: Because GDM is typically asymptomatic and cannot be reliably detected through clinical examination alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GDM produces no reliable clinical symptoms — it is detected entirely through systematic laboratory screening. Without a structured protocol, affected women would remain undiagnosed, exposing both mother and foetus to preventable complications.

answers.text: Because GDM exclusively affects women with a known family history of diabetes mellitus

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While family history is a risk factor, GDM can develop in any pregnant woman. Universal or risk-factor-based screening ensures that cases without obvious risk factors are not missed.

overallFeedback.feedback: GDM is defined as glucose intolerance first recognised during pregnancy. Because it is typically asymptomatic, it cannot be detected by clinical examination alone. This makes a structured antenatal screening protocol non-negotiable in every care programme.
Exactly right. The asymptomatic nature of GDM makes systematic screening the only reliable method of detection — clinical suspicion alone is insufficient.

params.question: Which statement best explains why delivery of the placenta is considered the only definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia?

answers.text: Because antihypertensive drugs become pharmacologically ineffective beyond 37 weeks of gestation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Antihypertensive drugs remain effective at any gestational age. However, they only lower blood pressure without addressing the underlying placental pathology that drives pre-eclampsia.

answers.text: Because the placenta is the source of the disease process, and all other interventions only stabilise the mother temporarily

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Pre-eclampsia originates from abnormal placentation. Antihypertensive therapy lowers blood pressure and MgSO4 prevents seizures, but both are temporising measures. Only removal of the placenta addresses the root cause of the disease.

answers.text: Because magnesium sulphate cannot be safely administered for more than 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MgSO4 can be administered for the duration clinically indicated, provided toxicity markers are monitored (knee jerk, respiratory rate, urine output). The reason delivery is definitive is that the placenta — not drug duration — is the source of disease.

answers.text: Because pre-eclampsia resolves spontaneously once the foetus reaches viability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pre-eclampsia does not resolve on its own regardless of foetal maturity. It can worsen rapidly at any gestational age, which is why the timing of delivery is a critical clinical decision balancing maternal and foetal risks.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pre-eclampsia is driven by factors released from an abnormally implanted placenta. Antihypertensives stabilise blood pressure and MgSO4 prevents seizures, but neither treats the underlying cause. Only delivery — specifically, removal of the placenta — is curative.
Precisely. Antihypertensives and MgSO4 are essential temporising measures, but delivery of the placenta is the only intervention that removes the source of the disease.

interactions.label: In a pregnant woman with a blood pressure reading of 150/95 mmHg recorded once i

params.question: In a pregnant woman with a blood pressure reading of 150/95 mmHg recorded once in the supine position, a diagnosis of gestational hypertension can be confirmed.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Two diagnostic errors are embedded in it: (1) BP in pregnancy must be measured sitting or semi-recumbent, never supine, because aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus produces artefactual readings; and (2) two BP readings at least four hours apart are required for diagnosing gestational hypertension — a single reading does not meet the diagnostic threshold.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false for two reasons. First, blood pressure must NEVER be measured in the supine position during pregnancy because the gravid uterus compresses the aorta and inferior vena cava, producing artefactual readings. The correct positions are sitting or semi-recumbent. Second, a single elevated reading is insufficient — two readings taken at least four hours apart are required before gestational hypertension can be diagnosed.
